text: Lesson 26 covered QLoRA — quantizing a frozen base model so it fits in memory while fine-tuning. This lesson covers a related but distinct use of quantization: compressing a finished model so it serves faster and cheaper. The underlying math overlaps, but the goal and the tradeoffs being made are different enough to separate clearly.

An 8-billion-parameter model is roughly 16 gigabytes in bf16 before any KV cache is counted. Quantizing to 8-bit or 4-bit cuts that footprint by 2 to 4x, which does three things at once: a bigger model fits on a given GPU, the freed memory serves a larger KV cache and more concurrent requests, and since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, moving fewer bytes per weight can directly speed up generation.

Three approaches dominate today. bitsandbytes quantizes on the fly at load time — simplest, but not always fastest. GPTQ is calibration-based: it uses a small dataset to minimize the rounding error introduced per layer, rather than rounding naively. AWQ is also calibration-based, but specifically protects the subset of weights that activations show matter most, quantizing the rest more aggressively.

Loading a model someone already quantized is straightforward — point AutoModelForCausalLM at a pre-quantized checkpoint on the Hub with device_map set to auto, and Transformers detects the quantization config and dispatches to the right kernels automatically. No separate conversion step needed on the loading side.

The tradeoff never disappears: 4-bit accuracy loss is usually small but measurable, and it grows at more aggressive bit widths or on tasks that depend on precise, multi-step reasoning. Always re-run the same eval set used on the full-precision checkpoint before shipping a quantization level, rather than trusting memory and latency numbers alone. Next up: turning these memory and throughput numbers into an actual dollar estimate for serving cost.
